key_terms.meaning: A body whose shape and size do not change under load, so the distance between any two of its points stays fixed.
The straight line drawn through a force along its direction; the force pushes or pulls along this whole line.
A vector that may be shifted anywhere along its own line of action without changing its external effect; a force on a rigid body is one.

key_terms.term: Moment of a force about a point
key_terms.meaning: M = r × F, where r is the position vector from the point O to any point on the line of action and F is the force; unit N·m.
The perpendicular distance d from the point to the line of action; magnitude of moment = F × d.

key_terms.term: Moment of a force about an axis
key_terms.meaning: M_axis = (r × F) · n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector along the axis; only the component of the moment along that axis survives.
M_AB = n̂ · (r × F), written as a 3×3 determinant of the unit vector, a position vector from any point on the axis, and the force.
M_O(F) = M_O(F₁) + M_O(F₂) + …, i.e. the moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about the same point.
Two forces equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and parallel but with different lines of action.
M = F × d, where F is the magnitude of either force and d is the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action; independent of the reference point.
A vector whose effect does not depend on where it is placed; a couple moment is a free vector.
A force F moved to a new point O together with the couple M = r × F that the shift creates.
Two force systems are equivalent when they have the same total force ΣF and the same total moment ΣM about every point.
The single force R = ΣF placed on a line of action chosen so that its moment about a reference point equals the total moment of the system.
The force or moment that a support supplies to stop the motion it prevents; a roller gives one unknown, a pin two, a fixed support three (in a plane).
A body loaded at exactly two points and in equilibrium; the two forces must be equal, opposite and collinear.
A body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces; the three lines of action must be concurrent or all parallel.
An imaginary, infinitesimally small displacement given to a system that its supports allow, with time frozen and real forces unchanged.
For a system in equilibrium, the total virtual work δU = Σ Fᵢ · δrᵢ is zero for every admissible virtual displacement.
The number of independent displacements a system can make; it sets how many independent virtual displacements you may choose.

takeaways: Transmissibility lets you slide a force along its own line of action, so only the line matters for the outside world — never slide it sideways.
A moment about a point is a vector r × F; its magnitude is F·d and its direction is the axis about which the force tends to turn the body.
The moment about an axis is just the projection of the moment vector onto that axis, found quickly with a scalar triple product.
Varignon's theorem turns an awkward inclined force into two easy perpendicular components, one of which usually has zero moment arm.
A couple has a moment but no net force, and that moment is the same about every point, which is why it is called a free vector.
Any force system reduces to one resultant force at a chosen point plus one couple; special cases collapse it into a single force or a pure couple.
Supports buy freedom with reactions: roller 1, pin/hinge 2, fixed 3 unknowns in a plane — count them before writing equations.
Equilibrium of a rigid body means ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any one point; in three dimensions that is six scalar equations.
A two-force member carries force only along the line joining its two pins; a three-force body in equilibrium has its three lines of action concurrent or parallel.
Virtual work removes the support reactions from the calculation, so a problem with many unknowns can be solved with one scalar equation.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on the free-body diagram first, then on correct vector working — showing ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 (or the equivalent force-couple reduction), with units and directions stated at the end.

bank.q: State the principle of transmissibility. Explain why it is valid for a rigid body but not for a deformable body or a body where internal effects matter.
outline: Statement: a force may be moved along its line of action without changing the external effect on a rigid body.
Reason: the external effect is fixed by the force vector and its line of action, and a rigid body transmits load without changing shape.
Counter-example: a rod pulled at one end versus pushed at the other has the same external reactions but opposite internal tension/compression.
Consequence: forces on rigid bodies are sliding vectors, not free vectors.

bank.q: Define the moment of a force about a point and about an axis. Write the vector expressions, name every term, and give the SI unit.
outline: M_O = r × F with r the position vector from O to any point on the line of action.
Magnitude M = F·d, d the perpendicular distance (moment arm).
M about axis with unit vector n̂: M = n̂ · (r × F).
Units: newton metre (N·m); direction by right-hand rule.
Zero cases: line of action passes through the point, or is parallel to the axis.

bank.q: State Varignon's theorem and show, with a diagram, how it is used to take the moment of an inclined force about a point.
outline: Theorem: moment of a force about a point = sum of moments of its components about the same point.
Resolve F into F cos θ and F sin θ at the point of application.
Add each component's moment with its own sign, using its own perpendicular distance.
Sign convention (anticlockwise positive) stated once and kept throughout.
Works for any number of components and in three dimensions.

bank.q: What is a couple? Prove that the moment of a couple is the same about every point in space, and explain why the couple moment is called a free vector.
outline: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action.
Take moments about an arbitrary point O: the terms containing r cancel, leaving M = F × d.
Result depends only on F and the perpendicular distance d, not on O.
Hence the couple moment can be drawn anywhere; it is a free vector.
A couple produces rotation only, no translation, because ΣF = 0.

bank.q: List the common types of supports and the number and nature of reactions each provides in two dimensions.
outline: Roller / rocker / frictionless slider: one reaction, normal to the surface.
Pin or hinge: two reactions, usually H and V.
Fixed (built-in) support: two forces plus one moment (three unknowns).
Cable or short link: one force along the link, tension only.
Smooth contact surface: one normal reaction (no friction).
Statical determinacy comment: unknowns versus available equations.

bank.q: A system of four coplanar non-concurrent forces acts on a plate. Reduce the system to a single force and a couple at the origin, then find the resultant and the point where its line of action cuts a chosen axis.
outline: Resolve every force into x and y components; sum to get Rₓ and R_y.
Resultant magnitude R = √(Rₓ² + R_y²) and direction θ = tan⁻¹(R_y/Rₓ).
Compute the total moment about O as Σ of (x·F_y − y·F_x) for each force.
Place R at distance d from O so that R·d equals that moment: d = M_O/R.
State the quadrant of the line of action correctly; check with a sketch.

bank.q: A simply supported beam of span L carries an inclined point load at distance a from the left end and a uniformly distributed load over part of the span. Draw the free-body diagram and find all support reactions.
outline: FBD: beam isolated, loads drawn, reactions at the pin (two) and roller (one).
Replace the UDL by its resultant at the centroid of the loaded length.
Resolve the inclined load into horizontal and vertical components.
ΣFₓ = 0 gives the horizontal reaction; ΣM = 0 about one support gives the other vertical reaction.
Verify the third equation ΣF_y = 0 as a check, quote answers with units and directions.

bank.q: A force F acts at a point A in space. Given the coordinates of A and two points B and C that fix an axis, find the moment of F about the axis BC.
outline: Write r from B (any point on the axis) to A.
Unit vector n̂ along BC from the coordinates of B and C.
Evaluate the 3×3 determinant n̂ · (r × F).
The sign tells the sense of rotation about the axis; magnitude in N·m.
Note that any point on the axis may be used for r and the answer is unchanged.

bank.q: A bent frame is loaded at three points. Using the two-force member idea, identify which members are two-force bodies, then find the remaining reactions.
outline: Free-body diagrams of each member drawn separately.
Members with pins at both ends and no intermediate load are two-force bodies; force along the pin-to-pin line.
Direction assumed arbitrarily, result sign interpreted (negative = opposite).
Equilibrium of the whole frame and of individual members used together.
Newton's third law pairs at the shared pin kept equal and opposite.

bank.q: A ladder rests against a smooth wall and on a rough floor. Using the principle of virtual work, find the force needed to hold it, or the angle at which it slips.
outline: Give the ladder a small virtual rotation δθ.
Write the virtual displacement of each load point in terms of δθ (position coordinates differentiated).
Set δU = Σ F · δr = 0; reactions at smooth wall and floor do no work.
Solve the single resulting equation for the unknown.
Compare with the equilibrium-equation solution to confirm.

bank.q: A force is shifted from point A to a parallel position at point O. Show what must be added to keep the system equivalent. Discuss the special outcomes when the added couple is zero or when the force is zero.
outline: Adding at O a force −F at A and +F at O leaves the system unchanged.
The pair (−F at A, +F at O) is a couple with moment M = r × F.
Equivalent system: F at O plus the couple M.
If r is parallel to F, M = 0 and the force may be moved as if along its line of action.
If the original system has ΣF = 0 but ΣM ≠ 0, reduction gives a pure couple, not a single force.
General case of a single force plus a parallel couple moment is the wrench.

bank.q: Show that a body in equilibrium under three coplanar non-parallel forces must have the three lines of action concurrent, and use the result to solve a three-force bracket problem.
outline: Take moments about the intersection point of two of the forces.
Those two forces give zero moment, so the third must also give zero moment.
Therefore the third line of action passes through the same point (or all three are parallel).
Apply to the bracket: reaction at the roller and at the pin, plus the applied load.
Solve by force triangle or by the concurrency point; verify with ΣM = 0.

bank.q: Compare the method of virtual work with the direct equilibrium equations for a linkage or machine. State when each is faster, and give the limitations of virtual work.
outline: Virtual work needs one scalar equation and eliminates ideal reactions; good for many-link systems.
Equilibrium equations need the whole FBD and a solution of simultaneous equations; they also give the reactions.
Virtual work needs a kinematically admissible displacement, so a mechanism study is unavoidable.
It does not give internal forces or reactions that do no work.
Choice depends on what is asked: input force only, or all reactions.

bank.q: A rigid body in space has more unknown reactions than the six equilibrium equations can supply. Explain how such a case arises, how you would check statical determinacy, and what the six equations are.
outline: ΣF = 0 gives three scalar equations; ΣM about a point gives three more.
Unknowns: each reaction component and moment component counted.
Determinate if unknowns equal independent equations; indeterminate if greater.
Classic causes: built-in supports at both ends, three or more parallel reactions, redundant links.
Indeterminacy resolved only by considering deformation (compatibility).
Mention partial constraints and improper supports, where equilibrium is impossible.

glossary.def: A body whose points keep fixed distances from one another under load.
The infinite straight line along which a force acts.
The rule that a force may slide along its line of action without changing its external effect on a rigid body.
A vector whose line of action is fixed but whose point of application along that line may change.
The perpendicular distance from a point or axis to the line of action of a force.
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to r × F and measured in N·m.
The component of the moment vector along a given axis, n̂ · (r × F).
A way to fix the sense of a moment vector: curl fingers from r to F, the thumb gives the direction.
The moment of a resultant about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about that point.
A pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces that produce rotation but no translation.
The moment of a couple, F × d, identical about every point in space.
A vector whose effect is unchanged when it is moved anywhere in space; a couple moment behaves this way.
A force together with a couple, obtained when a force is shifted to a parallel position.
Two force systems that give the same resultant force and the same moment about every point.
The single force (and possibly couple) that replaces a whole system of forces.
The simplest reduction of a general space force system: one force plus a couple moment parallel to it.
A sketch of the isolated body showing all applied loads and all support reactions.
The force or moment a support exerts to prevent the motion it restrains.
A case in which the unknown reactions equal the number of independent equilibrium equations.
A body loaded only at two points, so that the two forces must be equal, opposite and collinear.
A coplanar body in equilibrium under three forces, which must be concurrent or parallel.
An imaginary infinitesimal displacement allowed by the supports, with real forces unchanged.
The work done by real forces during a virtual displacement, δU = Σ F · δr.
The number of independent displacements a system can undergo.
